subject: Cognitive Science
title: Conditional Reasoning
description: A quick, practical guide to Conditional Reasoning.

hook.text: "If it rains, the ground is wet." The ground is wet. Did it rain? Not necessarily—maybe the sprinkler ran.

buildup.text: Conditional reasoning deals with if-then statements. Two valid forms: modus ponens and modus tollens.

discovery.text: Modus ponens: if P then Q; P is true; therefore Q. Modus tollens: if P then Q; Q is false; therefore not P.

twist.text: Two common errors: affirming the consequent and denying the antecedent. Both feel logical but aren't.

climax.text: Medical diagnosis is conditional reasoning: if disease X, then symptom Y. Symptom Y doesn't prove X.

punchline.text: "If-then" is simple. Getting it right is not.

quiz.question: What is affirming the consequent?
options: Assuming P is true because Q is true in an if-then rule

details.summary: Conditional reasoning involves if-then statements. Logically, 'if P then Q' only fails when P is true and Q is false. But people struggle with this, often committing errors like affirming the consequent or denying the antecedent. Abstract conditionals are especially difficult.
details.whyItMatters: Conditionals are everywhere in law, science, and daily reasoning. Misunderstanding them leads to invalid conclusions that feel perfectly logical.
takeaways: If-then logic fails only when the condition is met but the result is not
Affirming the consequent is a common invalid inference
Familiar content dramatically improves conditional reasoning

faq.question: What is affirming the consequent?
faq.answer: If it rains, the street is wet. The street is wet, therefore it rained. This is invalid because other things can wet the street. People commit this error constantly because it feels like valid backward reasoning. The correct reverse inference requires ruling out all other possible causes.

faq.question: Why do people reason better with familiar content?
faq.answer: Familiar content activates relevant knowledge that guides reasoning. You know streets can be wet from sprinklers, so you avoid the rain fallacy. With abstract symbols like P and Q, you have no such knowledge to draw on, and pure logical structure alone is cognitively demanding.
